opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we get a lot, because not everyone wants to pretrain from scratch.

The way I think about it comes from the nested learning view. A Transformer is already a special case of this multi-level system. Attention acts like a short-term memory that updates with the context, and the MLP blocks are a long-term memory that only updates during pretraining and then freezes. So with a pretrained model, you're not throwing anything away. You already have two levels of memory, and the question is how to add the levels in between.

In practice, the most natural choice is to keep attention as your highest-frequency component and turn the MLP blocks into what we call a continuum memory system. Instead of one frozen MLP, you have a chain of MLP blocks, each updating at a different frequency. You can initialize those blocks from the pretrained MLP weights, so you start from all the knowledge the model already compressed. Then the fast-updating levels can adapt at test time, while the slowest levels stay close to the original pretrained knowledge.

A few design decisions really matter here:

- **How many levels you need.** This depends on the context lengths and kind of continual adaptation you care about.
- **Update frequencies, or chunk sizes.** These decide how often each level gets updated.
- **Which parameters you let move at test time.** If you make everything fast, you risk forgetting what the pretrained model knows. If everything is slow, you're basically back to a standard Transformer.

You also need some continued training so the model learns to use these new update dynamics. The pretrained model was never trained to modify its own weights in-context, so it needs time to learn how to do that well. But that's far cheaper than pretraining from scratch.

So my general advice is to treat the pretrained model as your slowest, most stable memory, and build the faster levels on top of it. That's the spirit of Hope. It's less about replacing the architecture and more about recognizing that the model is already a set of memories. You're just filling in the spectrum between "this conversation" and "everything I learned in pretraining."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a really practical question, and honestly it's one we think about a lot, because most people aren't going to pretrain a Hope model from scratch. They have a Llama or a Qwen checkpoint sitting there, and the question is how do you get the benefits of this nested, continual-learning structure without throwing away all that pretrained knowledge.

The way I frame it is that Hope is really a design space rather than a single architecture. You have these nested levels of optimization, each with its own update frequency, and the core idea is that different parts of the model learn at different timescales. So when you're starting from a pretrained model, the first thing I ask is: which part of this model do I want to keep frozen, or nearly frozen, as the slowest level? And usually the answer is the pretrained weights themselves. Those are your long-term memory. They were trained on trillions of tokens, they encode a huge amount of knowledge, and you don't want them being overwritten by whatever happened in the last few thousand tokens of context.

Then the question becomes where you insert the faster-adapting components. There are a couple of natural choices. One is to treat the attention layers as the fixed slow component and add a continuum memory block, something like the Titans-style neural memory, in parallel or in sequence, so that the fast weights handle in-context adaptation while the pretrained attention does what it already does well. The other option is to replace some fraction of the attention layers with these memory modules, which gets you better efficiency on long context, but you pay a cost because you're removing capacity the model was trained with and you need to do more adaptation to recover performance.

In practice I'd say start conservative. Keep the backbone intact, add the self-modifying components as additional modules, and give them a small warm-up phase where only those new parameters are trained. You want the pretrained model to see the memory as something it can read from without being disrupted by it initially. Then you gradually unfreeze and let the levels interact. If you jump straight to full joint training with aggressive inner-loop updates, you tend to see the fast components fight the slow ones and the model gets worse before it gets better.

The other thing I'd flag is that the frequency schedule matters more than people expect. The whole point of the continuum memory system is that you have a spectrum, not just "fast weights and slow weights." When you adapt a pretrained model, you're effectively inheriting the slowest frequency for free, and your job is to fill in the intermediate ones. So I'd think about what kind of information needs to persist across, say, a document versus a session versus a deployment, and match the chunk sizes of the update levels to those timescales. That's where a lot of the design judgment is, and it depends heavily on the use case rather than on anything intrinsic to the architecture.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the pretrained model and ask which parts of its architecture we want to preserve. If you change everything at once, you lose much of the benefit of starting from those weights, and you’re effectively back to training a new model.

So I think about it as a gradual transition. Keep the components that are compatible, introduce the Hope components where you want additional learning or memory, and then train the model to use them. The choice depends on your constraints: how much additional training you can afford, how much of the original model’s behavior you need to preserve, and what you want the new architecture to accomplish.

There isn’t necessarily one configuration that’s best for every pretrained model. The practical question is: what’s the smallest architectural change that gives you the capability you’re looking for?

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with the pretrained model and ask how much of it you want to preserve. If you want to reuse its capabilities with a limited training budget, you probably don’t want to change the architecture so dramatically that you have to relearn everything.

The way I think about Hope is in terms of components that learn at different frequencies. So the question becomes: which knowledge should remain relatively stable, and which parts should be able to adapt more quickly? You can keep the pretrained model as the slower, more stable component and introduce adaptive memory around it. But those components still need training to work together; adding a memory module doesn’t automatically mean the model knows how to use it.

So there isn’t one architecture I would recommend independently of the setting. The choice depends on the checkpoint, your training budget, and what kind of adaptation you need at deployment.
